fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Filming the Lunar Wave and Eclipses", "body": "Crrow777 describes the lunar wave, a rippling distortion Chance likens to tracking trouble on an old VHS tape, and says others have since caught it in front of the moon, Jupiter and Saturn, so it seems to follow the ecliptic. He rejects the plane explanation, saying he scanned the sky with binoculars and citing footage of a supersonic jet whose every wing and tail throws its own wave. He suspects the firmament, and reads the Psalm on Wernher von Braun's headstone as a nod to it. From years of filming eclipses he says the moon never shows up entering an eclipse, and credits the Vedic nodes Rahu and Ketu."}, {"title": "Doubting NASA's Pictures of Earth", "body": "Crrow777 argues that no one can be certain of even a continent's shape when every map projection differs, and that the familiar pictures of Earth from space are artist renderings. He says clouds were caught cloned in some of them, that the famous Earthrise image showed an Earth of the wrong size, with crop marks of a paste job visible once its levels were raised in Photoshop, and that NASA later cleaned up the files. Chance brings up the missing mission tapes and an astronaut saying the moon technology was destroyed. Asked how so many staff could be fooled, Crrow777 says most engineers were probably honest people doing compartmentalized jobs."}, {"title": "What It Costs to Keep Asking Questions", "body": "Crrow777 recalls rebutting, with an optics expert, a Huffington Post piece that mocked him and called his object a satellite 11,000 miles away. Science, he argues, is meant to invite challenge rather than dismiss anyone without a Harvard degree. He says his YouTube channel, then over 100,000 followers, was deleted over a lunar wave video he did not even shoot and restored three weeks later with his search results gutted, and that a show he did with a physician was removed. Running a private site, he says, went from about $100 in the 1990s to thousands, and Chance urges listeners to back the independent media they want to exist."}, {"title": "Choosing Hope Over the Nightly News", "body": "Chance asks what gives reason for hope in 2020, which he sees as a year of people stuck at home and set against each other by contradictory mask advice. Crrow777 says people he considers in the know expect big changes, and reads a high court ruling on the Electoral College and stories around the British royal family as possible signs the old order is shifting, while warning it could be a double reverse. He argues that corporate news programs people into despair, and that if you act like a beaten dog, you get what a beaten dog gets. Chance wonders whether collective belief steers the outcome."}, {"title": "Reaching Back to Things That Worked", "body": "Crrow777 argues that nature is perfect in its delivery, that the planet would return to one big animal reserve within a few hundred years if people disappeared, and faults science for trying to control nature and even the weather by brute force. Earlier peoples, he says, respected the natural world and sought balance, and people are now reaching back to what worked: the mechanical washing machine that lasted 35 years, the colorful cars of the '60s and '70s, the organic food of great-grandparents. Chance adds that learning to garden from grandparents is a race against time, and Crrow777 calls mountains of disposable masks an unsustainable model."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Crrow777 is a regular guy who's spent a lot of time behind a telescope, shooting the moon and other aerial objects. In recent years, he's become a podcast host where he challenges many ideas that most people take for granted, especially the idea of where we are and what this realm might be. In this episode we talk about some of the discoveries he's made and filmed, we point out some of the obvious lies from NASA, internet censorship and free speech, and plenty more.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Spagyrics as Nature's Own Chemistry", "body": "Crrow777 frames spagyrics as the forerunner of all chemistry, a natural science that only achieves what nature permits and that works mainly within the plant kingdom, even though modern chemistry gives it no respect. He ties it to a wider return to older ways as people tire of drugs and pharmaceuticals, and when Chance Garton raises the Gerson method, Crrow777 describes how it was outlawed soon after Max Gerson announced it and how Charlotte Gerson was pushed across the border to Tijuana to keep practicing."}, {"title": "Living Juice and the Right Tools", "body": "The juicing discussion gets practical. Crrow777 explains why the Gerson method approves only the Norwalk and the Pure Juicer, which chew the produce and then squeeze it in a cloth under a hydraulic press, instead of the hot blades and micro screens most machines use to shred every cell. He compares it to old cider presses, laments that forced pasteurization ended living cider, and argues that supplements are unnecessary when food is grown and eaten the way ancestors did, recalling that Gerson first noticed the worms leaving when chemical fertilizers arrived."}, {"title": "Paying Doctors to Keep You Well", "body": "Chance Garton brings up the old model in which a family paid a doctor a regular stipend to keep everyone healthy, and notes how paying only when sick flips the incentives of the whole system. Crrow777 adds that healers once went unpaid if they failed, mocks the idea of treating a foot without treating the body, and recalls a past guest saying no pharmaceutical has ever cured anyone. He stresses that people differ by blood type and ancestry, so one pill cannot fit everybody, and the same reasoning carries into a thoughtful exchange on plant-based eating versus carnism."}, {"title": "Sound, Cymatics and the Stars", "body": "After Chance describes the quick relief he felt within days of trying a biofield tuning fork, Crrow777 calls cymatics one of the most hidden sciences of all. He points to cymatic patterns carved into old cathedrals, accounts of ancient cultures healing with sound and water, and old claims that great stones were lifted by sound, and he proposes filming defocused stars at high magnification to match their patterns to known frequencies. Chance runs with the idea of a sky clock, linking Newgrange, the word disaster as a bad star, and Zoroaster as a rock star."}, {"title": "Common Sense and the Coming Era", "body": "Asked how listeners can become truth teachers, Crrow777 says common sense is what the modern world lost, belief is merely a choice that becomes hard to undo, and a naked-eye crater supposedly forty miles wide on a distant moon should give anyone pause. Chance recommends Crrow777's common law conversation with Clint Richardson before the talk turns to the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn at the winter solstice, which Crrow777 treats as the end of one era and the start of another, noting that 9/11 followed the previous one, while Chance reads Saturn and Jupiter as the Father and the Son."}]

fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "I filmed for years, and I came to the conclusion that nothing leaves our atmosphere, nothing.
